summary: OpenAI describes how it used population-level analysis of core dumps to diagnose and fix two unrelated crash causes in its Rockset-based ChatGPT data infrastructure: a bad Azure host with silent hardware corruption, and an 18-year-old race condition in GNU libunwind.

practices.reason: The described pipeline for automatically extracting registers, filtering false positives, and labelling crash populations from core dumps is a transferable diagnostic method an engineering team could run against their own crash data.
practices.quote: We had ChatGPT write a script that downloaded a prefix of each core file, extracted the registers, filtered known false positives using the logs, and automatically labeled the crash as return-to-null, misaligned-stack, or other.

practices.reason: Switching the C++ exception unwinder implementation from GNU libunwind to libgcc is a concrete runtime change reported to reduce lock contention at scale, though the benefit is tied to OpenAI's own large-VM infrastructure.
practices.quote: Our immediate mitigation was to switch from GNU libunwind to libgcc’s unwinder. That was a good trade on its own: libgcc’s implementation has benefited from a lot of work to reduce lock contention, which matters when scaling to large VMs.

practices.reason: A patch has been proposed upstream for a race condition in a widely used open-source library, relevant to any team combining frequent signal delivery with C++ exception handling but not yet a shipped, mandatory change for most users.
practices.quote: We also upstreamed a self-contained reproducer and a fix to GNU libunwind, and verified that the other unwinders don’t have a similar issue.
